key: Not interrupting heavenly ordinances, although she minisheth human generations. The last of endless morns that have departed, the first of those that come, Dawn brightly shineth.
s: As the fire is kindled and Savitar sends all creatures to work, the hymn turns to Dawn’s dealings with Gods and men; Sāyaṇa, on 1.124.2, reads her as helping the Gods’ rites like the Agnihotra with her light while wearing away the life of men.
src: Sāyaṇa, Vedārthaprakāśa on Rig Veda 1.124.2, sa.wikisource (printed edition not named), revision 368324 (2023)

evidence.words: "दैव्यानि व्रतानि देवसंबन्धीनि अग्निहोत्रादीनि कर्माणि … तानि कर्माणि "अमिनती अहिंसन्ती' भानप्रदानेनानुकूलं कुर्वती । तथा "मनुष्या मनुष्याणां "युगानि युगोपलक्षितान् निमेषादिकालावयवान् “प्रमिनती प्रकर्षेण हिंसन्ती आयुः क्षपयन्तीत्यर्थः
evidence.gloss: ‘The divine ordinances’ (vratas): rites belonging to the gods, the Agnihotra and the rest … those rites she does not harm (aminatī) but makes favourable by giving light; and ‘the yugas of men’: the divisions of time the yugas stand for, the blink of an eye and the rest, she destroys outright (praminatī); that is, she wears away their life.

reason: Key verse verbatim (verse.js ok, ref 1.124.2, at [123,2]), the whole verse. Sāyaṇa on 1.124.2 takes the divine vratas as the gods’ rites, the Agnihotra and the rest, which Dawn does not harm but makes favourable by giving light, and the ‘yugas of men’ as the small divisions of time she destroys, wearing away life (āyuḥ kṣapayantī); he adds a second option (separating couples) not used in the sentence, which gives only his first reading. Wilson’s rendering and note (dawn as the fit season of the rites) agree. Plain sense draws on 1.124.1 (fire kindled, Savitar sending bipeds and quadrupeds to labour); faithful.
